newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - AEA sees three tracks for progress.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - AEA sees three tracks for progress.

text.p: British science and nuclear technology company AEA Technology Plc said on Monday that its first year profits after privatisation last year were up 22 percent as it eyes three routes for future growth.

"I think we can see further growth coming both organically and from acquisitions...in some areas, I think particularly internationally, the idea of partnership is very attractive and I'm sure we'll develop that," chairman Sir Anthony Cleaver told Reuters.

AEA Technology saw operating profits for the year ending March 31, 1997, rise 22 percent to 24.1 million pounds ($39.9 million) as pretax profits rose to 18.5 million from 15.8 million on turnover of 264 million, up four percent.
The company, which was sold off from the state-owned Atomic Energy Agency last year, paid out a total dividend of 8.4 pence per share.
Shares were off three pence to 452 pence by 0830 GMT, off a high of 458 pence, in thin volumes as the rest of the market eased.
Cleaver said each potential acquisition would be taken on its own merits and that with gearing around 25 percent, "I think we have headroom if we find the right opportunity."
AEA Technology bought three businesses last year, in research, software supplies and low-level radioactive material transport.
Cleaver said the company also saw further possibilities for partnerships with other firms.

"We see opportunities for working with major companies...who have some aspect of their business where either we've got particular expertise or basically (they) don't want to do it in house any longer," he said.

AEA Technology saw business from its previous parent the UK Atomic Energy Authority slip last year but this was offset by a rise of 18 percent in turnover from the UK private sector and a 34 percent jump in business overseas, Cleaver said.
He said he was encouraged that the increase in profits had come from "better margins and also from those higher sales," not just from cutting costs.
He said he expected further cost cuts but not a major restructuring.
"I can't think of any business in which there isn't an opportunity to improve the cost side of the equation...I'm sure there are opportunities. What we don't see is major restructuring," he said.
Business currently is split around 50-50 between nuclear-related work and that outside the company's roots.
Looking ahead, Cleaver said "we haven't set a strict percentage but obviously there are in toto more opportunities outside the nuclear industry than there are inside."
The company said that the last year had been "an important one in setting down the foundations for sustainable growth."
It said technology costs should be reduced by a restructuring into three main business segments which should also bring "greater cohesiveness to the way customers are serviced."
It added that the nuclear industry would continue to offer opportunities in the UK and overseas, particularly in safety and risk assessment and in plant life extension.
"We'll simply look for where we can get the best return for shareholders," he said.
Cleaver added that 84 percent of employees had invested in the business and "that's probably one of the best indicators of confidence for the future." ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
